Gold price changes are about 'back to the basics.' When we trade, we exchange money, something we believe/expect to be a widely accepted means of exchange and represent the value (store of value) of the trade we are doing. When you 'know' there is (at least some) gold underpinning that money and, hence, that transaction, the confidence in the means of exchange should be high. That is what gold does. It has been the physical representation of the value underneath our transactions for thousands of years.
So, the current size of transactions and trade, often 'paid for' with debt, with relatively little gold underneath, is driving the relative value of gold. In 'Greshem's law,' bad money drives out good, which explains why so few transactions are done with gold, apart from practical issues.
This 'mechanism,' which is directly related to inflation, drives the relative value of gold. When the amount of 'bad,' or better 'abundant' money is high compared to that of 'good' or scarce money, in this case, debt vs. gold, the price appreciation will increase, and vice versa.
